Az Exa AI egy teljesen újraépített, neurális hálózatokon alapuló keresőmotor, amelyet kifejezetten AI-alkalmazások és nagy nyelvi modellek (LLM-ek) számára terveztek – nem hagyományos kulcsszavas keresésre, hanem szemantikai megértésre optimalizálva.

## Az alapvető neurális architektúra

Az Exa legfontosabb technológiai újítása egy **end-to-end neurális hálózat**, amelynek középpontjában egy ún. *link prediction transformer* áll. Ez azt jelenti, hogy az indexelés és a visszakeresés minden lépése neurális modelleken keresztül történik – szemben a hagyományos keresők (pl. Google) PageRank-alapú, link-gráf és kulcsszó-egyeztetéses megközelítésével. A rendszer az embeddingek (vektoros reprezentációk) segítségével tárolja a weboldalak szemantikai tartalmát, így a lekérdezések során nem szó szerinti egyezést keres, hanem fogalmi hasonlóságot.[1][2]

Az index folyamatosan frissül: a keresési index percenkénti frissítéssel biztosítja, hogy az AI-alkalmazások valóban naprakész információhoz jussanak. Az indexelés során az Exa automatikusan eltávolítja a navigációs elemeket, hirdetéseket és cookie-értesítőket, így csak a tiszta, tartalmi szöveg kerül be az adatbázisba – ez az előfeldolgozás index-időben, nem lekérdezés-időben történik, ami kulcsfontosságú a gyors válaszidő szempontjából.[3][2]

## Saját GPU infrastruktúra

Az Exa az iparágban szokatlan, merész döntést hozott: már a cég korai szakaszában (7-8 fős csapatnál) saját GPU-klasztert vásárolt ahelyett, hogy felhőszolgáltatókra támaszkodott volna. Jelenleg egy **144 db NVIDIA H200 GPU-ból** álló új klasztert és egy meglévő **80 db A100 GPU-s** klasztert üzemeltet párhuzamosan. Az infrastruktúra-stack öt rétegből áll: Pulumi (infrastruktúra-kód), Ansible/Kubespray (szerverkonfiguráció), NVIDIA operátorok, Alluxio (elosztott tárolás) és Flyte (ML-pipeline-ok orkesztrációja).[4][5]

## Lekérdezés-feldolgozás és keresési módok

Az Exa intelligensen kombinálja a neurális és a kulcsszavas keresést: a rendszer a lekérdezés jellegétől függően automatikusan választja ki a legjobb megközelítést. A természetes nyelvű kérdéseket a rendszer gépi reprezentációvá alakítja, és a transformer-architektúra segítségével szemantikai értelmet rendel hozzájuk, lehetővé téve az összetett, többrétegű kérdések feldolgozását is.[6]

## API-termékarchitektúra

Az Exa négy fő API-végpontot kínál fejlesztők számára, amelyek különböző AI-alkalmazási igényeket elégítenek ki.[4]

| Végpont | Kimenet | Felhasználási eset |
|---|---|---|
| `/search` (csak URL-ek) | URL-listák | Ultra-alacsony késleltetésű alkalmazások |
| `/search` (URL + tartalom) | URL + teljes Markdown szöveg | LLM-ek számára RAG pipeline-ok |
| `/answer` | Strukturált válasz vagy riport | Előfeldolgozott, kész válaszok |
| `/research` | Komplex struktúrált kimenet | Agentic, mélykutatási feladatok |

## Multi-agent kutatási rendszer

Az Exa `/research` végpontja egy **LangGraph-alapú multi-agent architektúrát** alkalmaz. Egy *Planner* ágens feldarabolja a komplex lekérdezést részfeladatokra, több párhuzamos *Task* ágens hajtja végre ezeket egyidejűleg Exa-kereséssel, majd egy *Observer* ágens összesíti és strukturált formátumban adja vissza az eredményeket. Ez az architektúra lehetővé teszi, hogy olyan kutatási kérdések is megválaszolhatók legyenek, amelyek egyetlen kereséssel nem oldhatók meg.[7]

## Integráció és skálázhatóság

Az Exa támogatja a **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** szabványt, ami azt jelenti, hogy AI-asszisztensek (pl. Claude) közvetlenül MCP-szerverként konfigurálhatják az Exát, és natív web-keresési képességet kapnak anélkül, hogy egyéni integrációt kellene fejleszteni. Intelligens gyorsítótárazási stratégiák csökkentik az API-költségeket és a késleltetést, időalapú érvénytelenítéssel biztosítva az adatok frissességét nagy terhelés esetén is. Az Exa célja összességében az, hogy az AI-rendszerek ne csak a tanítási adataikra támaszkodva, hanem valós idejű, magas minőségű webes információval kiegészítve működhessenek.[2][8]

entries.answer: A GitHub-repository tartalmát nem sikerült lekérni (valószínűleg privát a repo). Az alábbiakban az Exa-architektúra leírása alapján összeállítom a teljes, szigorúan technikai, produkciókész rendszerépítési promptot Zig nyelven – figyelembe véve a hat meglévő komponensed (tensor, memory, ranker, ssi, reasoning_orchestrator, c_api) neveit és várható szerepét, ahogyan azok egy neurális webes keresőrendszerben illeszkednek egymáshoz. *** ## A generált prompt *** Build a complete, production-ready, end-to-end neural web search infrastructure entirely in the Zig programming language (targeting Zig 0.13 or later stable release). The system must encompass every subsystem described below, with no placeholder, stub, mock, simulated, or incomplete code permitted anywhere. Every file must be fully implemented with real, functional logic. *** ### Project Structure The project root must contain a `build.zig` that compiles the entire system as a set of library modules and a standalone executable binary. The module dependency graph must be explicitly declared. The directory layout must be: ``` src/ core/ tensor.zig memory.zig index/ ssi.zig ranker/ ranker.zig core_relational/ reasoning_orchestrator.zig c_api.zig crawler/ crawler.zig html_parser.zig link_extractor.zig embedding/ transformer.zig tokenizer.zig positional_encoding.zig search/ query_processor.zig neural_retriever.zig keyword_retriever.zig hybrid_router.zig pipeline/ indexing_pipeline.zig query_pipeline.zig server/ http_server.zig api_router.zig response_serializer.zig cache/ lru_cache.zig time_invalidation.zig agent/ planner.zig task_agent.zig observer.zig orchestrator.zig storage/ inverted_index.zig vector_store.zig document_store.zig util/ json.zig hash.zig arena.zig main.zig build.zig ``` *** ### 1. Core: `src/core/tensor.zig` Implement a fully generic, comptime-typed `Tensor(T)` struct that supports: - Arbitrary rank (shape described as a comptime or runtime slice of `usize`). - Contiguous row-major memory layout backed by a slice allocated through a provided `std.mem.Allocator`. - Methods: `init(allocator, shape)`, `deinit()`, `get(indices)`, `set(indices, value)`, `reshape(new_shape)` (zero-copy where possible), `slice(dim, start, end)`. - Element-wise operations: `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div` (both scalar and tensor–tensor, broadcasting along leading dimensions). - Reduction operations: `sum(dim)`, `mean(dim)`, `max(dim)`, `argmax(dim)`. - Matrix multiplication `matmul(a, b)` for rank-2 tensors with a BLAS-style inner loop, optimized with loop tiling (tile size 64). - Softmax over a specified dimension. - Layer normalization: given a tensor of shape `[..., d]`, compute mean and variance over the last dimension, normalize, then apply learnable `gamma` and `beta` parameters. - All operations must propagate errors via Zig error unions. No `unreachable` or `@panic` except in clearly documented invariant violations. *** ### 2. Core: `src/core/memory.zig` Implement a memory management module providing: - An `ArenaPool` that wraps `std.heap.ArenaAllocator` with reference counting, so multiple owners can share an arena and it is freed only when the last reference is released. - A `RingBuffer(T)` generic struct backed by a fixed-capacity heap array, supporting concurrent single-producer/single-consumer access using Zig's `std.atomic` primitives (`AtomicOrder.acquire`/`.release`). - A `SlabAllocator` for fixed-size object pools with a free-list, reducing fragmentation for frequently allocated small objects (e.g., index nodes, embedding vectors of a fixed dimension). - All allocators must implement the `std.mem.Allocator` interface so they are drop-in replacements. *** ### 3. Index: `src/index/ssi.zig` Implement a **Semantic Search Index (SSI)** that stores document embeddings and supports approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval: - The index must use **Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)** graph structure implemented from scratch in Zig. No external ANN library is permitted. - HNSW parameters: `M` (max connections per layer), `ef_construction` (search width during insertion), `ef_search` (search width during query), all configurable at init time. - Each node stores: a document ID (`u64`), a dense float32 embedding vector of dimension `D` (runtime parameter), and per-layer neighbor lists. - Insertion: assign a random layer using exponential distribution (`-ln(uniform) / ln(M)`), insert greedily from top layer down to layer 0. - Search: return the top-k nearest neighbors by cosine similarity using the HNSW `ef_search` beam. - Persistence: `save(path: []const u8)` serializes the entire graph to a binary file (little-endian, documented format); `load(path)` deserializes it back. - Thread-safety: use `std.Thread.Mutex` to guard concurrent insertions while allowing concurrent reads via reader-writer semantics (implement a simple `RwLock` using two atomics and a mutex if the standard library does not provide one). *** ### 4. Ranker: `src/ranker/ranker.zig` Implement a two-stage ranker: **Stage 1 — Coarse retrieval score:** Given a query embedding vector and a list of candidate document embeddings, compute cosine similarity scores in a vectorized loop (use SIMD via `@Vector` Zig builtins for f32 slices of length divisible by 8). **Stage 2 — Cross-encoder re-ranking:** Implement a lightweight cross-encoder that takes a concatenated `[query_tokens ++ sep_token ++ doc_tokens]` sequence, passes it through a small transformer encoder (4 layers, 256 hidden dim, 4 attention heads, configurable), and outputs a scalar relevance score via a final linear projection. Weights must be loadable from a flat binary file (float32, row-major). Provide `loadWeights(path)` and `saveWeights(path)`. The ranker must expose: - `rankCoarse(query_emb, candidates, top_k) → []ScoredDoc` - `rankCrossEncoder(query_tokens, doc_tokens_list, top_k) → []ScoredDoc` - `rankHybrid(query_emb, query_tokens, candidates, alpha, top_k) → []ScoredDoc` where `alpha` linearly interpolates coarse and cross-encoder scores. `ScoredDoc` must contain: `doc_id: u64`, `score: f32`, `rank: u32`. *** ### 5. Core Relational: `src/core_relational/reasoning_orchestrator.zig` Implement a reasoning orchestrator that executes a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of reasoning steps over retrieved document sets: - Define a `ReasoningNode` tagged union with variants: `Retrieve`, `Filter`, `Merge`, `Rank`, `Summarize`, `Extract`. - A `ReasoningPlan` is a list of `ReasoningNode`s with explicit data-flow edges (each node declares its input node indices). - The orchestrator executes the plan in topological order, using a thread pool (`std.Thread.Pool`) to run independent nodes in parallel. - `Retrieve` nodes invoke the neural retriever with a sub-query string. - `Filter` nodes apply predicate functions over `Document` structs (field: `url`, `title`, `body`, `pub_date`, `score`). - `Merge` nodes deduplicate and union document sets by `doc_id`. - `Rank` nodes invoke the ranker. - `Summarize` nodes apply a simple extractive summarizer: score sentences by TF-IDF, select top-N. - `Extract` nodes apply regex or structural field extraction from document body text. - The final result is a `ReasoningResult` containing an ordered list of `Document`s and a plain-text synthesized answer constructed by concatenating the top extracted sentences. *** ### 6. Core Relational: `src/core_relational/c_api.zig` Expose a stable C ABI from the entire system using `export` and `callconv(.C)`: ```c // Initialize and destroy the search system SearchSystem* search_system_init(const SearchSystemConfig* config); void search_system_destroy(SearchSystem* sys); // Index a document int search_index_document(SearchSystem* sys, const char* url, const char* title, const char* body, int64_t pub_timestamp_unix); // Execute a search query, returns JSON UTF-8 string (caller must free) char* search_query(SearchSystem* sys, const char* query, int top_k, int mode); // mode: 0 = auto, 1 = neural, 2 = keyword, 3 = hybrid // Execute a deep research query (multi-agent, blocking) char* search_research(SearchSystem* sys, const char* query); // Free a string returned by the API void search_free_string(char* ptr); ``` All structs passed across the boundary must be `extern struct` with explicit padding where necessary. All functions must be `export fn` with `callconv(.C)`. Error codes: 0 = success, negative = error (define an `ErrorCode` enum exported as `c_int` constants). *** ### 7. Crawler: `src/crawler/` **`crawler.zig`**: Implement an asynchronous, politeness-aware web crawler: - Use Zig's `std.http.Client` for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 GET requests with configurable timeout (connect: 5 s, read: 10 s). - Maintain a `CrawlQueue` backed by a priority queue ordered by estimated content quality score (initial score = 1.0 for seed URLs, decremented by link depth). - Respect `robots.txt`: fetch and parse `robots.txt` for each host before crawling; cache parsed rules per host with a 24-hour TTL. - Rate limiting: maximum 1 request per domain per second using a per-domain `TokenBucket` struct. - Deduplication: use a `BloomFilter` (configurable capacity and false-positive rate) to skip already-seen URLs. - Spawn up to `N` crawler worker threads (configurable), each pulling from the shared queue. **`html_parser.zig`**: Implement an HTML5 parser (subset sufficient for content extraction): - Tokenize the HTML byte stream into a flat list of `Token` (StartTag, EndTag, Text, Comment, Doctype). - Build a lightweight DOM tree (only element nodes and text nodes; discard comments). - Extract: `` text, all `<meta name="description">`, all `<h1>`–`<h3>` texts, all `<p>` texts, `<article>` body if present. - Strip all `<script>`, `<style>`, `<nav>`, `<footer>`, `<header>`, `<aside>` subtrees entirely. - Output: a `ParsedDocument` struct with fields `title: []u8`, `description: []u8`, `headings: [][]u8`, `paragraphs: [][]u8`, `clean_text: []u8` (concatenation of headings and paragraphs, separated by newline). **`link_extractor.zig`**: Extract and normalize all `` URLs from a parsed document: - Resolve relative URLs against the document's base URL. - Filter out `mailto:`, `javascript:`, `#fragment`-only, and non-HTTP(S) schemes. - Normalize: lowercase scheme and host, remove default ports, decode percent-encoding for unreserved characters, remove tracking parameters (`utm_*`, `fbclid`, `gclid`, `ref`). *** ### 8. Embedding: `src/embedding/` **`tokenizer.zig`**: Implement a Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizer: - Load a vocabulary file (JSON format: array of strings) and a merges file (text format: one merge rule `"a b"` per line). - `encode(text: []const u8) → []u32`: apply BPE to produce a token ID sequence. Pre-tokenize by Unicode word boundaries and punctuation splitting. - `decode(ids: []const u32) → []u8`: reconstruct the original text. - Add special tokens: `[PAD]=0`, `[UNK]=1`, `[CLS]=2`, `[SEP]=3`, `[MASK]=4`. - Maximum sequence length: 512 tokens (truncate if longer). **`positional_encoding.zig`**: Implement sinusoidal positional encodings: - Precompute a `[max_seq_len, d_model]` matrix using `PE[pos, 2i] = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model))`, `PE[pos, 2i+1] = cos(...)`. - Provide `addTo(embeddings: *Tensor(f32))` which adds the positional encoding in-place. **`transformer.zig`**: Implement a full transformer encoder from scratch: - `TransformerConfig`: `vocab_size`, `d_model`, `n_heads`, `n_layers`, `d_ff`, `max_seq_len`, `dropout_rate`. - Embedding layer: token embeddings (`[vocab_size, d_model]`) + positional encoding. - Each encoder layer: multi-head self-attention (with causal mask option) + feed-forward block (two linear layers with GELU activation) + pre-layer norm. - Multi-head attention: project Q, K, V with learned weights, split into heads, compute scaled dot-product attention (`softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V`), concatenate heads, project output. Apply dropout mask (for training mode; in inference mode, dropout is a no-op). - `forward(token_ids: []const u32, mask: ?[]const bool) → Tensor(f32)`: returns the last-layer hidden states of shape `[seq_len, d_model]`. - `embed(token_ids: []const u32) → Tensor(f32)`: returns only the embedding + positional encoding, without running encoder layers. - Weight loading: `loadWeights(allocator, path: []const u8)` reads a flat binary file of float32 values in the order: token_embeddings, then for each layer [q_weight, q_bias, k_weight, k_bias, v_weight, v_bias, out_weight, out_bias, ff1_weight, ff1_bias, ff2_weight, ff2_bias, norm1_gamma, norm1_beta, norm2_gamma, norm2_beta]. *** ### 9. Search: `src/search/` **`query_processor.zig`**: Parse and preprocess a raw query string: - Detect query type: `Natural` (contains a verb or question word), `Keyword` (short, no verbs), `URL` (starts with `http`). - Tokenize using the BPE tokenizer. - Expand synonyms using a static hash map (load from a JSON file at init time: `{ "term": ["syn1", "syn2"] }`). - Return a `ProcessedQuery` struct: `raw: []u8`, `tokens: []u32`, `type: QueryType`, `expanded_terms: [][]u8`. **`neural_retriever.zig`**: Encode the query with the transformer, then search the SSI: - Call `transformer.embed(query_tokens)` to get a `[seq_len, d_model]` tensor, then mean-pool over the sequence dimension to get a single `d_model`-dimensional query vector. - Call `ssi.search(query_vector, ef_search, top_k * 4)` to get candidate `doc_id` list. - Load document embeddings for candidates from the `VectorStore`. - Call `ranker.rankHybrid(...)` with configurable `alpha`. - Return top-k `ScoredDoc`s with full `Document` structs loaded from `DocumentStore`. **`keyword_retriever.zig`**: BM25 retrieval over the inverted index: - Implement BM25 scoring: `score(q,d) = Σ IDF(t) * (tf(t,d) * (k1+1)) / (tf(t,d) + k1*(1 - b + b*|d|/avgdl))` with `k1=1.5`, `b=0.75`. - Query the `InvertedIndex` for each query term, merge posting lists with score accumulation. - Return top-k `ScoredDoc`s. **`hybrid_router.zig`**: Decide which retrieval path to use: - If `ProcessedQuery.type == .Natural` → neural retriever. - If `ProcessedQuery.type == .Keyword` → keyword retriever. - If `ProcessedQuery.type == .URL` → direct document lookup by URL hash. - Otherwise → run both in parallel using `std.Thread.Pool`, then merge and re-rank with the cross-encoder. *** ### 10. Storage: `src/storage/` **`inverted_index.zig`**: A persistent inverted index: - In-memory: a hash map from term string to a posting list (`ArrayList` of `Posting{ doc_id: u64, tf: u32, positions: []u32 }`). - `addDocument(doc_id, tokens)`: tokenize and update postings. - `getPostings(term) → []Posting`. - `save(path)` / `load(path)`: binary serialization (little-endian). Format: 4-byte vocab size, then for each term: 2-byte term length, term bytes, 4-byte posting count, then each posting as `(u64 doc_id, u32 tf)`. - Compute and store global statistics: `total_docs: u64`, `avgdl: f64`, per-term `df: u32` for IDF. **`vector_store.zig`**: A flat file-backed store for dense float32 embedding vectors: - Fixed embedding dimension `D` set at init time. - `put(doc_id: u64, embedding: []const f32)`: append to a memory-mapped file. The file is an array of `(u64 doc_id, f32[D] embedding)` records. - `get(doc_id: u64) → ?[]const f32`: binary search by `doc_id` (records are sorted on flush). - `flush()`: sort records by `doc_id`, write to disk. **`document_store.zig`**: A key-value store mapping `doc_id` to full `Document`: - `Document` fields: `id: u64`, `url: []u8`, `title: []u8`, `body: []u8`, `pub_date: i64`, `score: f32`. - Use a memory-mapped append-only log file. Each record: 4-byte length prefix, then a packed binary encoding of the struct (all string fields as 4-byte length + bytes). - Maintain an in-memory `HashMap(u64, u64)` mapping `doc_id → file_offset` for O(1) lookup. - `put(doc: Document)`, `get(doc_id) → ?Document`, `saveIndex(path)`, `loadIndex(path)`. *** ### 11. Cache: `src/cache/` **`lru_cache.zig`**: A generic `LruCache(K, V)`: - Backed by a `HashMap` and a doubly-linked list. - `get(key) → ?V`: moves the accessed entry to the front. - `put(key, value)`: evicts the least-recently-used entry if capacity is reached. - `capacity: usize` set at init time. - Thread-safe via `std.Thread.Mutex`. **`time_invalidation.zig`**: Wraps `LruCache` with TTL: - Each entry stores a monotonic expiry timestamp. - `get` returns `null` and evicts if the entry is expired. - A background `std.Thread` runs every 60 seconds to sweep expired entries. *** ### 12. Agent: `src/agent/` Implement a multi-agent research system: **`planner.zig`**: Given a complex query string, decompose it into a list of `SubQuery` structs by: - Splitting the query on conjunctions (`and`, `also`, `as well as`, `furthermore`, `,`). - Generating one `SubQuery` per independent information need. - Each `SubQuery` has a `text: []u8` and a `priority: u8` (1–5). **`task_agent.zig`**: Executes a single `SubQuery`: - Calls the `HybridRouter` to retrieve documents. - Extracts key sentences using TF-IDF sentence scoring. - Returns a `TaskResult{ sub_query: SubQuery, documents: []Document, key_sentences: [][]u8 }`. **`observer.zig`**: Merges multiple `TaskResult`s: - Deduplicates documents by `doc_id`. - Re-ranks the merged document list using the cross-encoder with the original full query. - Synthesizes a final answer string by concatenating the top-5 key sentences from across all task results, in relevance order. - Returns `ObserverResult{ documents: []Document, answer: []u8 }`. **`orchestrator.zig`**: Wires planner, task agents, and observer: - `research(query: []const u8) → ObserverResult`: 1. Call `planner.decompose(query)` → `[]SubQuery`. 2. Spawn one `task_agent` goroutine per `SubQuery` using `std.Thread.Pool`. 3. Collect all `TaskResult`s. 4. Call `observer.merge(results, original_query)`. 5. Return the `ObserverResult`. *** ### 13. Server: `src/server/` **`http_server.zig`**: Implement an HTTP/1.1 server using `std.net.StreamServer`: - Accept connections in a thread pool (default 8 threads). - Parse HTTP/1.1 request line, headers, and body (support `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`). - Route requests to `api_router.zig`. - Keep-alive: honor `Connection: keep-alive` up to 100 requests per connection. **`api_router.zig`**: Implement four endpoints: `POST /search` — body: `{ "query": "...", "top_k": 10, "mode": "auto" }`: - Process query through `HybridRouter`. - Return JSON: `{ "results": [ { "url": "...", "title": "...", "score": 0.95, "snippet": "..." } ] }`. `POST /index` — body: `{ "url": "...", "title": "...", "body": "...", "pub_date": 1234567890 }`: - Run the indexing pipeline. - Return `{ "status": "ok", "doc_id": 12345 }`. `POST /answer` — body: `{ "query": "..." }`: - Run neural retrieval + extractive summarization. - Return `{ "answer": "...", "sources": [...] }`. `POST /research` — body: `{ "query": "..." }`: - Run the multi-agent orchestrator. - Return `{ "answer": "...", "documents": [...] }`. **`response_serializer.zig`**: Implement a minimal JSON serializer (no external library): - Support serializing `[]u8` strings (with proper UTF-8 escape sequences: `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\uXXXX` for non-ASCII control characters), `f32`/`f64` floats (6 decimal places), `i64`/`u64` integers, booleans, null, arrays, and objects. - Implement `JsonWriter` that writes directly to a `std.io.Writer`. *** ### 14. Pipeline: `src/pipeline/` **`indexing_pipeline.zig`**: Orchestrates end-to-end document indexing: 1. Receive a `RawDocument{ url, html_body, fetch_time }`. 2. Parse with `html_parser.zig` → `ParsedDocument`. 3. Assign `doc_id = hash64(url)`. 4. Tokenize `clean_text` with the BPE tokenizer. 5. Store in `DocumentStore`. 6. Update `InvertedIndex` with tokenized text. 7. Encode with the transformer (mean-pool) → embedding vector. 8. Store embedding in `VectorStore`. 9. Insert into SSI (HNSW). **`query_pipeline.zig`**: Orchestrates end-to-end query execution: 1. Check `LruCache` for the query string; return cached result if valid. 2. Call `QueryProcessor.process(raw_query)`. 3. Route through `HybridRouter`. 4. Populate `Document` structs from `DocumentStore`. 5. Store result in `LruCache` with 5-minute TTL. 6. Return `[]ScoredDoc` with full documents. *** ### 15. Utilities: `src/util/` **`json.zig`**: Implement a recursive-descent JSON parser: - `parse(allocator, input: []const u8) → JsonValue` where `JsonValue` is a tagged union of `Null`, `Bool(bool)`, `Int(i64)`, `Float(f64)`, `String([]u8)`, `Array([]JsonValue)`, `Object([]JsonField)`. - `JsonField{ key: []u8, value: JsonValue }`. - Full RFC 8259 compliance: all Unicode escapes, number formats. **`hash.zig`**: - `hash64(data: []const u8) → u64`: implement FNV-1a 64-bit hash. - `hash32(data: []const u8) → u32`: FNV-1a 32-bit. - `BloomFilter` struct: configurable bit array size and number of hash functions (use FNV-1a with different seeds per function). Methods: `add(item: []const u8)`, `mightContain(item: []const u8) → bool`. **`arena.zig`**: A per-request arena allocator wrapper: - `RequestArena.init(backing_allocator) → RequestArena`. - `RequestArena.allocator() → std.mem.Allocator`. - `RequestArena.reset()`: frees all allocations without freeing the backing buffer (reuse for next request). - `RequestArena.deinit()`: fully releases backing buffer. *** ### 16. `main.zig` Implement the program entry point: - Parse CLI arguments: `--config <path>`, `--port <u16>`, `--data-dir <path>`, `--model-weights <path>`, `--vocab <path>`, `--merges <path>`. - Load all configuration, initialize all subsystems in dependency order (memory allocators first, then storage, then transformer weights, then SSI, then ranker, then server). - Register a signal handler for `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` that calls a graceful shutdown sequence: stop accepting new connections, wait for in-flight requests (up to 5 s), flush the `InvertedIndex` and `VectorStore`, save the SSI HNSW graph, then exit. - Print startup diagnostics to stderr: loaded vocab size, HNSW node count, document count, listening address. *** ### Build: `build.zig` Use the Zig build system API: - Define a static library target `kissofdeath` that compiles all `src/**/*.zig` files. - Define an executable target `kissofdeath_server` that links the library and compiles `main.zig`. - Enable link-time optimization in `ReleaseFast` mode. - Export the C API header by generating `kissofdeath.h` from the exported symbols in `c_api.zig` using a build step that invokes `zig translate-c` or a custom header generation step. - Add test targets for each module under `src/` using `addTest`. *** ### Constraints Applicable to All Code - All memory allocation must go through an explicitly passed `std.mem.Allocator`; no global allocators. - All file I/O errors must be handled and propagated as Zig error union values. - No use of `std.debug.print` in production paths; logging must go through a `std.log`-compatible interface. - All public APIs must have doc comments (`///`). - Thread synchronization must use only `std.Thread.Mutex`, `std.Thread.Semaphore`, `std.atomic.Atomic`, or `std.Thread.Pool` from the standard library. - SIMD paths using `@Vector` must have scalar fallback paths for widths not divisible by the SIMD width. - The entire codebase must compile cleanly with `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` with zero warnings. *** Ez a prompt teljes mértékben lefedi a rendszer minden rétegét, a saját `tensor.zig`, `memory.zig`, `ranker.zig`, `ssi.zig`, `reasoning_orchestrator.zig` és `c_api.zig` komponenseidre támaszkodva, és egyetlen placeholdernek vagy mocknak sem hagy helyet – minden egyes modul valódi, produkciókész Zig implementációt követel meg.[1][2][3][4]

entries.query: az exa rust ban épült kezdjük ott xd én zig be akarom
entries.answer:
Igen, az Exa vektordatabázisa és a teljesítménykritikus szerveroldali komponensei (kiemelések szervere, lekérdezési pipeline) **Rust**ban íródtak  – és most te ugyanezt Zig-ben akarod megvalósítani. Ez egy nagyon érdekes és mérnökileg izgalmas döntés, ezért nézzük meg pontosan mit jelent ez a gyakorlatban.[1][2]

## Miért Rust az Exánál

Az Exa csapata eredetileg Pythonban írta a highlights szervert, majd **4×-es átviteli sebesség növekedést** értek el azzal, hogy átírták Rust-ba. A vektordatabázisuk webléptékű: klaszterezés, matryoshka embeddingek, bináris kvantizáció és **SIMD műveletek** kombinációját alkalmazzák, és ezt mind Rustban implementálták. Az Exa 2.0 kiadásakor új klaszterezési algoritmusokat, lexikális tömörítést és assembly-szintű optimalizációkat vezettek be – szintén Rustban.[2][1]

## Zig vs Rust erre a feladatra

Zig-ben teljesen megvalósítható mindaz, amit az Exa Rustban épített, sőt néhány területen Zig előnyösebb. Az alábbiakban a két nyelv összevetése az Exa-féle use case szempontjából:

| Szempont | Rust | Zig |
|---|---|---|
| SIMD támogatás | `std::arch`, `packed_simd` crate | Beépített `@Vector`, közvetlen SIMD vektorok natívan |
| Memory management | Ownership + borrow checker | Explicit allokátorok, `comptime` zero-cost absztrakció |
| C interop | `extern "C"`, FFI blokkok | Natív C header import (`@cImport`), zökkenőmentes |
| Build rendszer | Cargo (extern) | `build.zig` (beépített, scriptelható) |
| Async I/O | Tokio (extern runtime) | `std.net`, `std.event` – még fejlődő ökoszisztéma |
| Bináris méret | Közepes–nagy | Rendkívül kis bináris, no hidden runtime |
| Comptime | Nincs valódi megfelelője | `comptime` – fordítási idejű számítás, generics helyett |

## Mit kell Zig-ben megépíteni

Az Exa architektúrájából a következő komponenseket érdemes Zig-ben implementálni, a komplexitás sorrendjében:

**1. Vektoros hasonlóság-számítás (cosine similarity, dot product)** — Ez a legkritikusabb rész. Zig `@Vector(N, f32)` típusokkal és `@reduce` builtin-nel natív SIMD kód írható, amely az AVX-512 utasításkészletet közvetlenül kihasználja, fordítóra bízva a vektorizációt. A bináris kvantizáció (float32 → 1 bit) `@bitCast` és `@popCount` builtinekkel triviálisan megvalósítható.

**2. Inverted index és tömörített postings lista** — Delta encoding + Variable Byte encoding írható tiszta Zig-ben, `std.io.BitWriter`-rel. A trigram index a fuzzy kereséshez szintén beépíthető.

**3. Matryoshka embedding csonkítás** — Comptime-ban meghatározható, hogy a keresés melyik dimenzióban fusson (pl. 128d gyors előszűrés, 1536d re-ranking), és a struktúrák mérete fordítási időben fixálódik.

**4. HTTP szerver (Highlights server megfelelője)** — `std.net.StreamServer` + threadpool, vagy a `zap` / `http.zig` library-k egyike.

**5. HNSW gráf-alapú ANN keresés** — A Hierarchical Navigable Small World algoritmus Zig-ben implementálható `std.ArrayList` és `std.PriorityQueue` segítségével, a csomópontok memóriája custom allokátorral kezelhető.

## Konkrét Zig-specifikus előnyök

A Zig `comptime` mechanizmusa lehetővé teszi, hogy az embedding dimenzió, a kvantizációs szint és az index szegmens mérete **fordítási időben** legyen paraméterezhető – ezt Rustban generics + const generics kombinációjával lehet megközelíteni, de Zig-ben természetesebb a szintaxis. Az explicit allokátor-modell (`std.mem.Allocator` interfész) azt jelenti, hogy pontosan kontrollálható, mikor és hol allokál a vektordatabázis – ez nagy dokumentumszámnál (az Exa esetében ~20 milliárd dokumentum ) kritikus a GC-spike-ok elkerüléséhez.[3][2]

## Amire figyelj

Az ökoszisztéma lényegesen kisebb, mint a Rusté: nincs `tokio`-szintű async runtime, a `serde`-hez hasonló szintű JSON szerializáció még fejlődik, és a machine learning / BLAS integrációhoz saját C bindinget kell írni. Az Exa által használt GPU-s training pipeline (H200 klaszter, Flyte orkesztráció) Python/CUDA marad – Zig csak a **query serving réteg** nyelveként releváns, pontosan úgy, ahogy az Exánál is a Rust csak a szervizelési oldalon jelenik meg.[4]

entries.answer:
Elolvastam az összes komponensedet. Zseniális alap – most megírjuk a teljes promptot, ami pontosan hivatkozik a saját kódodra.

***

## A generált prompt

***

Build a complete, production-ready AI-powered semantic search engine with multi-agent deep research capabilities. The system is delivered in exactly two files: one backend (`main.zig`) and one frontend (`index.html`). All subpages must be within the single `index.html` using client-side routing. No stubs, mocks, placeholders, or simplified code are permitted anywhere.

***

### Backend: `main.zig`

The backend is a single Zig source file targeting **Zig 0.14.0**. It implements an HTTP server, all query processing logic, and all integrations with external AI embedding and LLM APIs. The following existing modules from the `kissofdeath` repository are imported and used directly — do not reimplement them, import them exactly as shown:

```zig
const Tensor        = @import("src/core/tensor.zig").Tensor;
const memory        = @import("src/core/memory.zig");
const Ranker        = @import("src/ranker/ranker.zig").Ranker;
const RankerConfig  = @import("src/ranker/ranker.zig").RankerConfig;
const SSI           = @import("src/index/ssi.zig").SSI;
const Orchestrator  = @import("src/core_relational/reasoning_orchestrator.zig").ReasoningOrchestrator;
```

#### Memory strategy

Use `memory.ArenaAllocator` for per-request allocation: each incoming HTTP connection creates one arena, all allocations for that request live in it, and the entire arena is freed when the response is sent. Use `std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator` as the backing allocator for the global SSI index, Ranker state, and Orchestrator state.

#### Global state (initialized at startup)

Initialize the following as global singletons before entering the accept loop:

- One `SSI` instance using the GPA allocator, loaded from `index.bin` if it exists on disk, otherwise initialized empty.
- One `Ranker` instance using the GPA allocator, with `num_ngrams = 6`, `num_hash_funcs = 128`, `seed = 0xdeadbeefcafebabe`. If `ranker.bin` exists on disk, call `ranker.importModel("ranker.bin")` to restore weights.
- One `Orchestrator` instance using the GPA allocator.
- Two comptime constants loaded from environment variables at startup using `std.process.getEnvVarOwned`: `EMBED_API_KEY` (used for OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint) and `LLM_API_KEY` (used for OpenAI chat completions).
- `EMBED_URL`: environment variable, default ``
- `EMBED_MODEL`: environment variable, default `text-embedding-3-small`
- `EMBED_DIM`: environment variable parsed as `usize`, default `1536`
- `LLM_URL`: environment variable, default ``
- `LLM_MODEL`: environment variable, default `gpt-4o`

#### HTTP server

Use `std.net.StreamServer` bound to `0.0.0.0:8080`. Accept connections in a loop. Spawn a `std.Thread` per connection. Parse the HTTP request manually: read until `\r\n\r\n`, extract method, path, headers, and Content-Length. Read the body if Content-Length > 0. Route by `method + path` to the handler functions below. All responses use HTTP/1.1 with `Content-Type: application/json` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` headers on every response. Respond to `OPTIONS` on any path with `204 No Content` and the CORS headers.

#### Embedding helper function

Implement `fn getEmbedding(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) !Tensor`. This function:

1. Builds a JSON body: `{"model": "<EMBED_MODEL>", "input": "<text>", "encoding_format": "float"}`. Escape the `text` string for JSON (handle `"`, `\`, newlines, and non-ASCII bytes).
2. Opens a TLS connection to the embedding endpoint host using `std.crypto.tls.Client` over `std.net.tcpConnectToHost`. Sends an HTTP/1.1 POST with `Authorization: Bearer <EMBED_API_KEY>`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `Host`, `Content-Length`, and `Connection: close` headers.
3. Reads the full response body, extracts the `data[0].embedding` array from the JSON using a hand-written parser (scan for `"embedding":[` then parse comma-separated float strings until `]`).
4. Allocates a `Tensor` of shape `&.{EMBED_DIM}` using the provided allocator, fills its `data` slice with the parsed floats, returns it.

#### LLM helper function

Implement `fn callLLM(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, system_prompt: []const u8, user_prompt: []const u8) ![]u8`. This function:

1. Builds a JSON body with `model`, `messages` array containing a system message and a user message, `max_tokens: 2048`, `temperature: 0.2`. Escape all string fields for JSON.
2. Opens a TLS connection to the LLM endpoint host, sends an HTTP/1.1 POST with the same auth headers as the embedding function.
3. Reads the response, extracts `choices[0].message.content` by scanning for that key in the JSON, returns the content as an allocated `[]u8`.

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/index`

Handler receives a JSON body: `{"id": "string", "url": "string", "title": "string", "text": "string"}`.

1. Parse all four fields from the JSON body (hand-written scan for `"id":`, `"url":`, `"title":`, `"text":` keys).
2. Concatenate `title + " " + text` into a single string, then tokenize it: split on whitespace and punctuation, lowercase each token, hash each token with `std.hash.Wyhash.hash(0, token_bytes)` cast to `u32`, producing a `[]u32` token array.
3. Call `ssi.addSequence(tokens, position=0, anchor=false)` where position is `0`.
4. Call `getEmbedding(arena_allocator, concatenated_text)` to get a `Tensor`.
5. Store the embedding in a global `std.StringHashMap(Tensor)` keyed by `id`, protected by a `std.Thread.Mutex`. The value `Tensor` must be allocated with the GPA allocator (copy from arena to GPA before inserting).
6. Store the document metadata `{id, url, title}` in a global `std.StringHashMap(DocMeta)` where `DocMeta = struct { url: []u8, title: []u8 }`, also GPA-allocated.
7. Respond `{"status": "indexed", "id": "<id>"}` with HTTP 200.

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/search`

Request body: `{"query": "string", "top_k": <integer, default 10>, "mode": "hybrid|neural|keyword", "rerank": <bool, default true>}`.

1. Parse all fields.
2. Tokenize the query string using the same tokenizer as `/api/index`.
3. If `mode` is `"keyword"` or `"hybrid"`: call `ranker.topKHeap(&ssi, query_tokens, top_k * 3, arena_allocator)` to get `[]types.RankedSegment`. For each segment, attempt to find the matching document by computing `stableHash(segment.tokens[0..min(4, len)], seed)` and looking up the SSI. Build candidate `[]DocResult` from matched documents.
4. If `mode` is `"neural"` or `"hybrid"`: call `getEmbedding(arena_allocator, query_string)` to get a query `Tensor`. Iterate all stored embeddings in the global map. For each, call `Ranker.vectorScore(&stored_emb, &query_emb)` and collect `DocResult` entries with the cosine similarity score.
5. If `mode` is `"hybrid"`: combine scores from steps 3 and 4 by summing them per document ID (weight: 0.5 keyword + 0.5 neural), deduplicate by ID.
6. If `rerank` is true: call `ranker.rankCandidatesWithQuery(candidates, query_tokens, &ssi, arena_allocator)`.
7. Take the top `top_k` results sorted by descending score.
8. Respond with:
```json
{
  "query": "string",
  "mode": "string",
  "total": <int>,
  "results": [
    {"id": "string", "url": "string", "title": "string", "score": <float>}
  ]
}
```

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/answer`

Request body: `{"query": "string", "top_k": <integer, default 5>, "mode": "hybrid|neural|keyword"}`.

1. Call the `/api/search` logic internally (reusing the same code path, not via HTTP) to retrieve `top_k` documents.
2. Fetch the full stored text for each result from the document metadata map. If original text is not stored (only title/url available), use `title` as the context snippet.
3. Build a context string:
   ```
    <title>\nURL: <url>\nContent: <text up to 1500 chars>\n\n ...
   ```
4. Call `callLLM(arena_allocator, system_prompt, user_message)` where:
   - `system_prompt` = `"Answer the question using only the provided sources. Cite each source inline as [1], [2], etc. Be precise and complete."`
   - `user_message` = `"Question: <query>\n\nSources:\n<context>"`
5. Respond with:
```json
{
  "query": "string",
  "answer": "string",
  "sources": [{"index": 1, "id": "string", "url": "string", "title": "string"}]
}
```

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/research`

Request body: `{"query": "string", "num_subtasks": <int, default 4, max 8>, "results_per_task": <int, default 5>}`.

This endpoint implements a three-phase planner–executor–synthesizer pipeline entirely in Zig:

**Phase 1 — Plan:**
Call `callLLM` with a system prompt instructing the model to decompose the query into exactly `num_subtasks` sub-questions as a JSON array of strings: `["sub-question 1", "sub-question 2", ...]`. Parse the returned JSON array by scanning for `[` and extracting quoted strings until `]`.

**Phase 2 — Execute:**
For each sub-question (executed sequentially — Zig threads are optional here):
1. Run the `/api/search` logic for that sub-question with `top_k = results_per_task` and `mode = "hybrid"`.
2. Build a source context string from the returned results.
3. Call `callLLM` with a system prompt: `"Synthesize a focused answer to the sub-question from the provided sources. Cite inline."` and user message containing the sub-question and the source context.
4. Store `{subtask: string, answer: string, sources: [{id, url, title}]}` in a `std.ArrayList`.

**Phase 3 — Synthesize:**
Build a combined context from all subtask answers and call `callLLM` with system prompt: `"Write a comprehensive research report in Markdown. Structure: Executive Summary, Detailed Findings (one subsection per sub-question), Conclusion, Bibliography."` The user message contains all subtask answers concatenated.

Respond with:
```json
{
  "query": "string",
  "final_report": "string (Markdown)",
  "subtask_results": [
    {"subtask": "string", "answer": "string", "sources": [{"id": "string", "url": "string", "title": "string"}]}
  ],
  "total_sources_consulted": <int>
}
```

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/similar`

Request body: `{"id": "string", "top_k": <int, default 10>}`.

1. Look up the stored embedding `Tensor` for the given `id`.
2. Iterate all other stored embeddings, compute `Ranker.vectorScore` against the reference embedding.
3. Sort by score descending, return top `top_k`, excluding the document with the same `id`.
4. Respond with the same structure as `/api/search`.

***

#### Endpoint: `POST /api/train`

Request body: `{"sequences": [["tokens as strings"]], "labels": [<floats>], "epochs": <int, default 10>}`.

1. Parse the array of token string arrays, hash each token to `u32` using the same tokenizer, build `[][]u32`.
2. Call `ranker.calibrateWeights(training_data, labels, &ssi, epochs)`.
3. Call `ranker.exportModel("ranker.bin")`.
4. Respond `{"status": "trained", "epochs": <int>, "weights_saved": true}`.

***

#### Endpoint: `GET /api/health`

Respond `{"status": "ok", "indexed_documents": <int>, "ssi_segments": <int>, "timestamp": "<RFC3339>"}` where `indexed_documents` is the count of entries in the document metadata map, `ssi_segments` is `ssi.segments.count()`, and `timestamp` is the current UTC time formatted manually as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.

***

#### Error handling

All handlers must catch every possible error. On any error, respond with HTTP 400 or 500 and body `{"error": "<error name>", "detail": "<optional string>"}`. Never let an unhandled error propagate past the per-connection thread function — catch everything with `catch |err|` and write a 500 response.

***

### Frontend: `index.html`

Single self-contained file. All CSS in one `<style>` block. All JavaScript in one `<script>` block before `</body>`. Zero external dependencies — no CDN, no external fonts, no external scripts. All icons are Unicode or inline SVG. All views are `<div>` elements toggled by a JS router keyed on `window.location.hash`.

#### Constants

At the top of the script block:
```js
const API_BASE = '';
```

#### Design system

- Background: `#09090b`
- Surface: `#18181b`
- Border: `#27272a`
- Accent: `#6366f1`
- Accent hover: `#4f46e5`
- Text primary: `#fafafa`
- Text muted: `#71717a`
- Success: `#22c55e`
- Error: `#ef4444`
- Font: `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif`
- Monospace: `'JetBrains Mono', 'Fira Code', 'Casc
